name: Sugar scrub / pumice exfoliation

lead: Scrubbing with sugar, salt, a loofah or pumice rubs off dead skin so rough patches feel smoother straight away and skin looks softer and brighter. People also use it before and after shaving or waxing to help prevent ingrown hairs, though reference sources on that benefit are weakly referenced.

The abrasive physically sloughs off the outer layer of dead skin cells. Pumice, a porous volcanic rock, has been used on skin and hair since ancient Egypt, Rome and China. No clinical trials of sugar scrub or pumice were found.

paras: Scrubs are rubbed in circular motions on softened skin in the shower; pumice is used mainly on calluses and corns after soaking. Loofahs need regular cleaning and replacing.

Dermatologists cited by Wikipedia say manual exfoliation is not medically necessary because dead cells shed naturally. Too much can break the skin barrier, causing redness, tightness, sensitivity and possible infection. Loofahs can harbour bacteria and fungi if not cleaned.

angle.text: Scrubbing with sugar or pumice rubs off dead skin so rough patches feel smoother right away and skin looks softer and brighter, and helps keep hairs from getting trapped after hair removal. Dermatologists describe it as not medically necessary.

lead: Sugar scrub and pumice exfoliation are forms of mechanical exfoliation, which removes dead surface skin by rubbing with an abrasive. For appearance, people use scrubs to leave skin feeling smoother and look fresher, to even the texture of rough areas, to soften calluses and to reduce ingrown hairs where hair is shaved or waxed. Wikipedia describes exfoliation as used in facials to promote skin regeneration and deep cleansing, through mechanical or chemical means [1].

Tools include microfibre cloths, microbead scrubs, crushed nut shells, sugar or salt, pumice, sponges, loofahs and brushes [1]. Pumice is a lightweight porous volcanic rock used as a mild abrasive for dead skin and unwanted hair [2]. Exfoliating before and after hair removal is presented as a step to prevent ingrown hairs in reference sources, though that article is weakly referenced [3].
Dermatologists cited in the exfoliation article say it is not medically necessary, since dead skin cells shed naturally [1]. No clinical trials of sugar scrub or pumice were found.

paras: Scrubs may be sugar, salt, nut-shell or plastic microbead based. Microbead scrubs use small plastic spheres; they pass through sewage works and harm marine ecosystems, and Illinois banned them in June 2014, with many countries restricting them since [1]. Exfoliation nets are nylon mesh tools native to Ghana that dry faster than sponges [1]. Wet shaving and waxing also exfoliate, with manual razors more effective than electric ones [1].

Pumice is fairly abrasive and is used mainly on calluses and corns, usually after soaking [1]. The exfoliation article advises people with dry skin to avoid scrubs with a lot of pumice [1]. Other exfoliation types include chemical peels using alpha or beta hydroxy acids, dermaplaning, dermabrasion and laser resurfacing [1].

Exfoliation is said to have been practised by the ancient Egyptians, who used animal oils, alabaster, salt and sour milk, and in China during the Qing dynasty [1]. Pumice was used in ancient Egypt with creams and razors for hair removal, in Rome in powdered form for toothpaste, and in China for nails and calluses; a Roman poem from around 100 BC describes it removing dead skin [2].

Exfoliation is described as promoting skin regeneration and deep cleansing [1]. Ingrown hairs are most common where skin is shaved or waxed, and exfoliating before and after hair removal is suggested as prevention, using scrubs, gloves, loofahs or brushes. The article presenting this is flagged as weakly sourced; its cited studies concern razor bumps in the beard area [3].

Excessive exfoliation can break the skin's barrier against microorganisms, possibly leading to infection, tightness, sensitivity and redness, and can worsen dry, flaky skin [1]. Loofahs can harbour bacteria and fungi; the article advises drying after use, weekly cleaning and replacement every three to four weeks [1]. Finely ground pumice in toothpaste is described as too abrasive for daily use [2].
No studies found. The Wikipedia article on exfoliation carries a banner noting that it needs more reliable medical references [1].

timeline.event: A Roman poem describes pumice removing dead skin [2].
Exfoliation used in China during the Qing dynasty [1].
William Tilbury Fox develops phenol peeling to reduce the appearance of freckles [1].
Illinois bans plastic microbeads, followed by restrictions elsewhere [1].
